rejected.title: Creating hybrid texts
card: A hybrid text mixes the structures or features of two or more text types or modes. One example is a story told through text messages, emails and photos.
Each part does a job. A text message can show a quick, casual voice. A photo can show a place or mood without any description.
Writers choose which forms to mix by thinking about the audience. A story for teenagers might use a group chat, while a story for young children might use pictures and short captions.
The mix should still make sense as one text. Each part should move the story or idea forward, not just add decoration.
rejected.remember: A hybrid text blends forms, and each form is chosen for its job and its audience.

a.q: What makes a text a hybrid text?
opts: It blends features of two or more text types or modes
It is written in two different languages
It is retold from a different point of view
It is adapted from a book into a film
a.why: A hybrid text mixes the structures or features of different text types or modes, such as emails and photos in one story. Retelling from another point of view changes the narrator, not the forms used.
a.clue: Think about mixing forms inside one text.

b.q: Jo is writing a mystery for Year 7 readers. She tells it through a group chat, a school notice and a photo of a muddy footprint. Why is this a good choice for her audience?
opts: The forms are familiar to readers and each adds a clue
Mixing forms lets the story skip a plot and characters
The photo is decoration that makes the page look less plain
The forms suit adult readers who enjoy complex layouts
b.why: Jo picks forms her Year 7 readers know, and each one has a job: the chat gives voices, and the notice and photo give clues. The photo is not just decoration, because the footprint moves the mystery forward.
b.clue: Ask what each form does for the reader.
